name: Pinkish Brown
lede: Pinkish brown is a plain descriptive name for a muted rosy brown, and in the books it turns up as the color a fading red dye left behind.

sections.title: A color that dyes decayed into
sections.body:
Brazilwood gave deep crimson and purple dyes, but they usually faded quickly to what Greenfield calls a dowdy pinkish brown [1]. Brazilwood was often castigated as a false color for that reason, and it also tended to stiffen cloth [1]. Because good red dyestuffs were rare, brazilwood stayed valuable anyway [1]. Greenfield adds that when new varieties of the wood turned up in South America, the whole region was named Brazil [1].

Birren, writing in 1950, reports that Japanese tradition held a red or pinkish-brown cat in the greatest dread, among a list of animal omens [2]. It is an isolated report and is best read as folklore rather than a rule about the color.

sections.title: The swatch and the picture archive
sections.body: The swatch here is a screen color, not a dye [3]. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of it covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 304 works [3]. It clusters in Indian painting: 104 of the 721 Indian works carry it, and 25 of the 96 Kalighat paintings [3]. The strongest single case is Émile Bernard's *Symbolic Self-Portrait* of 1891 [3]. As always these are photographs of varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors [3].

notes.cite: Birren, Color Psychology and Color Therapy, ch. 3 ("The Amulet Wearers")

questions.q: What did brazilwood dyes usually fade to?
True or false: brazilwood stayed valuable because good red dyes were rare.

openers: Brazilwood reds usually faded to a dowdy pinkish brown, and the name Brazil comes from the dyewood.
